newsitem.title: MALAWI: Trade body concerned as Mozambique plans to quit.
newsitem.headline: Trade body concerned as Mozambique plans to quit.

text.p: A top official of the Common Market for Eastern and Southern Africa (COMESA) said Mozambique had given notice of its plan to withdraw from the 20-nation African trade group and appealed to it to reconsider.
Bingu wa Mutharika, COMESA's secretary general, said Mozambique would lose out in regional trade projects.

"It is much of a surprise because COMESA is in the best interest of Mozambique. We still don't understand what was the motive. My only advice is that they reconsider their position," he told Reuters on Wednesday.
Mozambique's foreign minister Leonardo Simao said his country had suspended participation in COMESA in December. The country intends to withdraw formally at the end of 1997.
"We are not interested in participating in COMESA. We have suspended our participation," he told Maputo's daily Noticias last month.

"Even when COMESA was created we had some reservations, because our volume of cooperation with many countries in the organisation was negligible. We just signed adhesion to the COMESA treaty, but we have never ratified it," he said.
Mozambique's immediate interest lay with the Southern African Development Community (SADC), he said.
Lesotho also announced in December it would withdraw from COMESA because it was a member of SADC and felt that the two bodies performed similar functions.
But Mutharika believed Mozambique's war-torn economy could benefit from COMESA which was formed to promote trade in its member states.
He said the body had received in 1996 aid pledges for the next two years worth between $500 million and $700 million for regional projects.
He added that COMESA was shocked that Mozambique, which needed to secure a regional export market while rehabilitating its industries, had decided to pull out.

With donor support, Mutharika said, COMESA had lined up regional projects like Automated System of Customs Data (ASYCUDA) and Common External Tarriff (CET) to protect local industries from foreign competition.
Also planned was a deal with Euro Trace, a statistical data base for international trade, and Trade International Network (TINET) to join telephone networks in member states.

"We're trying to make the telephone systems in the region compatible because there is no way we can develop ourselves if we cannot communicate" he said, adding that Mozambique would be able to benefit from these industrial developments.

The pullout of Mozambique would not impact on its neighbours Malawi and Zambia who are also COMESA members because many of the corridors like Nacala and the northern corridor in Mozambique were run under separate projects outside the regional grouping, Mutharika said.
Simao said Mozambique preferred to work alongside the smaller 12-member SADC grouping.
"We should concentrate on SADC rather than joining an institution with a lot of members and where there is conflict between the members.
"Experience shows that the smaller the organisation, the better it functions," he said.

The COMESA states are Angola, Burundi, Comoros, Eritrea, Ethiopia, Kenya, Lesotho, Madagascar, Malawi, Mauritius, Mozambique, Namibia, Rwanda, Sudan, Swaziland, Tanzania, Uganda, Zaire, Zambia and Zimbabwe.
The SADC members are Mauritius, Angola, Lesotho, Swaziland, Zambia, Zimbabwe, Namibia, Mozambique, Tanzania and Malawi, South Africa and Botswana.
